Task 1a: Morphological Vessel Operations¶

Look at the research paper provided on Canvas and go to Page 3. This paper is the extension of the research paper you saw in Project 1.

  • Download the images, lesions and masks
  • Go to page 3 of the paper, column 2 and you will find this description: "Due to the narrowness of the vessels, all the vessel masks are dilated with a 3 × 3 structuring element and closed with a 2 × 2 structuring element, as shown in Fig. 4. This dilation prevents the vessels in the masks from being broken when augmented. Since the goal is to identify vessels within the lesion, the vessel masks are multiplied with U-Net-generated lesion masks to yield vessels only within the lesion. For both models, the images were square-cropped and then resized to 448 × 448."
  • Apply these steps to the 3 vessel masks and lesions provided and generate the final dilated, closed masks within the lesions.
In [1]:
#load in the pictures
import cv2
import numpy as np
from google.colab.patches import cv2_imshow
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt
from PIL import Image, ImageFilter
from google.colab import files

vessel1 = cv2.imread('/content/br042208rol367_CNP_vessel_mask.JPG')
vessel2 = cv2.imread('/content/hp041808rol363_NCP_vessel_mask.JPG')
vessel3 = cv2.imread('/content/rf071808rol439_CNP_vessel_mask.jpg')

legion1 = cv2.imread('/content/br042208rol367_CNP_legion_mask.JPG')
legion2 = cv2.imread('/content/hp041808rol363_NCP_legion_mask.JPG')
legion3 = cv2.imread('/content/rf071808rol439_CNP_legion_mask.jpg')

#convert to grayscale
vessel_gray1 = cv2.cvtColor(vessel1, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
vessel_gray2 = cv2.cvtColor(vessel2, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
vessel_gray3 = cv2.cvtColor(vessel3, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

#convert to grayscale
legion_gray1 = cv2.cvtColor(legion1, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
legion_gray2 = cv2.cvtColor(legion2, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
legion_gray3 = cv2.cvtColor(legion3, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
In [2]:
#Convert to binary
ret1, vessel_thresh1 = cv2.threshold(vessel_gray1, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)
ret2, vessel_thresh2 = cv2.threshold(vessel_gray2, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)
ret3, vessel_thresh3 = cv2.threshold(vessel_gray3, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)

ret4, legion_thresh1 = cv2.threshold(legion_gray1, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)
ret5, legion_thresh2 = cv2.threshold(legion_gray2, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)
ret6, legion_thresh3 = cv2.threshold(legion_gray3, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)

#Perform dilation
kernel = np.ones((3,3),np.uint8)
vessel_dilation1 = cv2.dilate(vessel_thresh1,kernel,iterations = 1)
vessel_dilation2 = cv2.dilate(vessel_thresh2,kernel,iterations = 1)
vessel_dilation3 = cv2.dilate(vessel_thresh3,kernel,iterations = 1)

#Perform closing on each image using a 2x2 struct element
kernel2 = np.ones((2,2),np.uint8)
vessel_closing1 = cv2.morphologyEx(vessel_dilation1, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, kernel2)
vessel_closing2 = cv2.morphologyEx(vessel_dilation2, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, kernel2)
vessel_closing3 = cv2.morphologyEx(vessel_dilation3, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, kernel2)

final_mask1 = cv2.bitwise_and(vessel_closing1, legion_thresh1)
final_mask2 = cv2.bitwise_and(vessel_closing2, legion_thresh2)
final_mask3 = cv2.bitwise_and(vessel_closing3, legion_thresh3)

#plot final masks
fig, axs = plt.subplots(3,1, figsize=(10, 10))
axs[0].imshow(final_mask1, cmap='gray')
axs[1].imshow(final_mask2, cmap='gray')
axs[2].imshow(final_mask3, cmap='gray')
plt.show()

Task 1b: Finding largest vessles¶

  • Choose the vessel file: rf071808rol439_CNP.jpg and apply all the operations you applied to it in Task 1a. While applying closing you might want to increase the kernel element structure size to see better closed vessels and not have too many broken vessels. The paper used a value of 2 because it had a different objective than what we are trying to achieve here.
  • Now use the connected components methodoly to find the number of connected vessels. Call the function to display the labeled image. You will see a colorful image
  • Our goal now is to create a binary image that only shows us the largest vessel. In this particular image, the largest (spanning the most pixels) connected vessels are the group on the top right, green in color (look at the connected vessels image provided for reference). We need to go from this to biggest_vessel.PNG, thats what we need to create. Here are some hints on how to do this:
  • The labels_im variable gives you the numpy array for the oringinal image with every pixel having the label of which component it belongs to. You can use np.unique to figure out how many unique labels there are (you can use a variation of np.unique to figure out pixel count for each label). For my code, I have 48 unique labels on the image. Also, as an example, the label 0 appears on 519172 pixels, which denotes the largest connected component in the image, the area without the vessels
  • Now in order to find the largest vessel you have to find the 2nd largest group of pixels belonging to a label
  • Once you have found the 2nd largest pixel value belonging to a label, find that label and use np.where to create an image where only the pixels belonging to the largest vessels are white and rest everything is black, the final output image is given for reference. Dsiplay the final image
In [3]:
vessel = cv2.imread('/content/rf071808rol439_CNP_vessel_mask.jpg')
vessel_gray = cv2.cvtColor(vessel, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

#Convert to binary
ret, vessel_thresh = cv2.threshold(vessel_gray, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)

#perform dilation
kernel = np.ones((3,3),np.uint8)
vessel_dilation = cv2.dilate(vessel_thresh,kernel,iterations = 1)
#perform closing
kernel2 = np.ones((6,6),np.uint8)
vessel_closing = cv2.morphologyEx(vessel_dilation, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, kernel2)

#connected components
num_labels, labels_im = cv2.connectedComponents(vessel_closing)
print("Number of connected components:", num_labels)

def imshow_components(labels):
    # Map component labels to hue val
    label_hue = np.uint8(179 * labels / np.max(labels))
    blank_ch = 255 * np.ones_like(label_hue)
    labeled_img = cv2.merge([label_hue, blank_ch, blank_ch])

    # cvt to BGR for display
    labeled_img = cv2.cvtColor(labeled_img, cv2.COLOR_HSV2BGR)

    # set bg label to black
    labeled_img[label_hue==0] = 0

    plt.imshow(cv2.cvtColor(labeled_img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB))
    plt.axis('off')
    plt.show()

imshow_components(labels_im)

#adjust function to only show the label we want
def imshow_components_specific(labels, target_label):
  binary_mask = np.where(labels == target_label, 255, 0).astype(np.uint8)
  plt.imshow(binary_mask, cmap='gray')
  plt.axis('off')
  plt.show()
imshow_components_specific(labels_im, 14)

#upload file
lic_date = files.upload()
license_plate_classifier = cv2.CascadeClassifier(next(iter(lic_date)))

def plt_show(image, title='', gray=False, size=(100,100)):
  temp = image
  if gray==False:
    temp = cv2.cvtColor(image, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)
    plt.title(title)
    plt.imshow(temp, cmap='gray')
    plt.show()
def detect_number(img):
  temp = img
  gray = cv2.cvtColor(temp, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
  number = license_plate_classifier.detectMultiScale(gray, 1.2)
  print("Number plate detected:"+str(len(number)))
  for num in number:
    (x,y,w,h) = num
    roi_gray = gray[y:y+h, x:x+w]
    roi_color = temp[y:y+h, x:x+w]
    cv2.rectangle(temp, (x,y), (x+w, y+h), (0,255,0), 3)
  plt_show(temp)

Task 2b: LICENSE PLATE DETECTION USING HAAR CASCADES: Analysis¶

  • The code should work properly on Car1 but fails to work on Car2. Can you explain why?
    Hint: This chunk of code below can provide us with the answers. Read the comments I have provided to think and explain what might be happening with Car2's implementation not working properly
In [14]:
for c in contours1:  # contours is a list of detected contours, which are essentially the boundaries of detected objects. The loop iterates through each contour to find the one that looks like a rectangle (four-sided polygon).
    # approximate the contour
    peri = cv2.arcLength(c, True)  # computes the perimeter (arc length) of the contour c
    approx = cv2.approxPolyDP(c, 0.018 * peri, True) #The second argument (True) indicates that the contour is closed (a complete loop).Cv2.approxPolyDP() simplifies the contour to fewer points.

    # if our approximated contour has four points, then
    # we can assume that we have found our screen
    if len(approx) == 4: #The second argument (0.018 * peri) controls the approximation accuracy: A lower value keeps more detail.The third argument (True) ensures the approximated contour remains closed.
                            # If the approximated contour has exactly 4 points, it is assumed to be a quadrilateral (rectangle/square).
        screenCnt1 = approx
        break
In [15]:
for c in contours2:  # contours is a list of detected contours, which are essentially the boundaries of detected objects. The loop iterates through each contour to find the one that looks like a rectangle (four-sided polygon).
    # approximate the contour
    peri = cv2.arcLength(c, True)  # computes the perimeter (arc length) of the contour c
    approx = cv2.approxPolyDP(c, 0.018 * peri, True) #The second argument (True) indicates that the contour is closed (a complete loop).Cv2.approxPolyDP() simplifies the contour to fewer points.

    # if our approximated contour has four points, then
    # we can assume that we have found our screen
    if len(approx) == 4: #The second argument (0.018 * peri) controls the approximation accuracy: A lower value keeps more detail.The third argument (True) ensures the approximated contour remains closed.
                            # If the approximated contour has exactly 4 points, it is assumed to be a quadrilateral (rectangle/square).
        screenCnt2 = approx
        break

Task 2b: Answer here

Car2 image fails here because the model is unable to detect the 4 points that would make up the license plate window. This is evident by new image 2 above showing a random piece of the car rather than the plate.
